_comment: The people of the Confluence village. spot names a place in the village layout (Core/Town/Village.cs). talk lines are tried in order and the first whose 'when' holds is said; 'when' can test quest (with state none/active/done, stage, ready) and flag. Each choice can start or advance a quest and has an optional reply. A Goodbye answer is always added. All names are placeholders. 'menu' in 'when' marks a page of the talk (a choice with do {"menu": "shop"} turns to it; "" goes back). do {"trade": {take, give, short}} swaps items with a seller: there is no money on Aruun yet, so sellers barter. A spot ending in '*' places the person at every spot that starts that way (food_stall* = the food stall in every town).

talk.say: You came up out of the ground with the hum gone quiet behind you. You woke the heart already, didn't you? Tell me.

choices.text: I woke it. The sentinel is broken.

talk.say: A stranger, with sky-dust still on you. Sit, if you like. Since you fell, the old stone to the south has been humming. The builders left a shrine there, buried. Nobody here can read their words any more.

choices.text: I'll go and see what's humming.
choices.reply: Follow the paved road south. Read what is carved before you speak; the old words answer only those who listen first.
Nobody knows. Whoever they were, they were here long before any of us, and their words still move stone.
The Teshari Confluence. Rest here whenever you need; the walls keep the night off.

talk.say: The road south leads to the arch. Read the carvings with care, and when a word comes to you, speak it where the stone can hear.

choices.text: How do I speak a word?
choices.reply: Say it toward the thing you mean it for. (Press X, pick the word with its number, then Enter.)

talk.say: The hum has stopped. You went all the way down, didn't you?

choices.text: The heart fell. It said: the world remembers.
choices.reply: I don't know what that means. Nobody does. But the hum has stopped, and you came back. Keep these, for the road.

talk.say: The old stone to the south is quiet now. You did that. The village is yours as much as ours.
Hungry? Everyone's hungry. The redstriders came close to the village this season, but nobody has had time to hunt. Bring me four cuts of raw meat and I'll make it worth your while.

choices.reply: Strike from the side, not the front. And mind the herd: if one runs, they all do.

talk.say: That smell! You've brought it?

choices.reply: Wonderful. Take some back, cooked properly, and a fire kit for the road.

talk.say: Four cuts of raw meat, friend. The redstriders graze the grass just outside the village.
The hearth's never been so full. Come by when you're hungry.
Something walks the grass at night: big, quiet, all teeth. I'm out of arrowheads. Eight pieces of flint and I can watch for it properly.

choices.reply: Grey nodules, on rocky ground. You can pick them up by hand.

talk.say: Is that flint I hear clacking in your bag?

choices.reply: Good stone. Here, a pick of my own making. Rock gives way to it.

talk.say: Eight pieces of flint. Grey nodules on rocky ground.
You've a good eye for stone. There's a steading past the wall, south-east, off the ruin road. Empty as long as I've kept the watch. The carved stone in its yard held a Tether once.

choices.text: Could I make it my home?
choices.reply: Set a new Tether on that stone and it's yours. Walls need mending, mind.

talk.say: I saw the light take, out past the wall. So the old place has someone again.

choices.reply: Then you'll want to mend it. Take this stone and timber; I won't be needing it.

talk.say: The steading's south-east, past the wall. Set a Tether on the carved stone in the yard.
Quiet night so far. If you see eyes in the grass, come back to the fire.

'Tomato'? Not Avarra, and not any Vaari word I know. A few old human families keep words like that, from wherever they lived before. If such a thing grows on Aruun at all, it grows where the world is thin and two places touch. The college would rather people did not go looking.

choices.reply: Tell her, then. And be careful where you look.

talk.say: You went down to the heart, didn't you? Tell me everything you saw. Every carving, every word. I will write it down.

choices.reply: Each ring is one word, copied as the builders carved it. Read the same words in the ruins and they will start to mean something to you.

talk.say: Quietly, please. This is the Grand College library. Everything we know of the builders' words is on these shelves, and most of it we cannot read.

choices.reply: Each ring is one word, copied as the builders carved it. Read the same words in the ruins and they will start to mean something to you.

choices.text: Can you teach me the words?
choices.reply: Nobody teaches them. You read them where they were carved, in two different places, and then you try them. The elder at the Confluence will tell you where to start.

talk.say: Everything's made this mornin'. I don't sell yesterday's, and I don't sell anything I wouldn't feed my own. Bring me the makin's and I'll cook it proper.

choices.text: Reed flatbread x2, for 3 reed stalks.

trade.short: Reeds, love. I can't bake bread out of wishes.

choices.text: Redroot stew x2, for 3 redroot and a glasswort leaf.

trade.short: Not enough for a pot yet.

choices.text: Redstrider pie x2, for 2 raw meat and 2 redroot.

trade.short: A pie with no filling is just a hat.

choices.text: Grandmother's soup, for 2 redroot and a glasswort leaf.

trade.short: Gran's soup gets proper makin's or none at all.

talk.say: Is that... oh. Oh, look at the colour of it. Is that a real one?

choices.text: A tomato, from where the veil was thin.
choices.reply: Generations my family's been writin' 'tomato' and cookin' redroot instead. Sit down. Sit! You're eatin' first. And I'm keepin' every last seed.

talk.say: Any luck? Gran's book says they're red and round and 'taste like summer'. Whatever summer is.

choices.text: Where did your family come from?
choices.reply: From the other side, a long way back. They came through when the veil was thin, with a stewpot and Gran's book and not much else. I've never seen it and I don't need to: Aruun's home. But the recipes remember where we started.

talk.say: Ilen keeps the college library. If anyone knows an old word, it's Ilen. Ask about 'tomato'.

You've a good nose for fresh things. Can I show you somethin'? This is Gran's cookbook. Her gran's, really, and back and back. Some of the words in it nobody knows any more. Look here: 'tomato'. Half the soups in this book start with it.

choices.reply: That's just it! My family's always used redroot instead. Gran swore the real ones still grow, wherever the world wears thin. Go and ask Ilen at the college library what the word means. If I could make Gran's soup the way it's written, just once...

choices.text: Where did your family come from?
choices.reply: From the other side, a long way back. They came through when the veil was thin, with a stewpot and Gran's book and not much else. I've never seen it and I don't need to: Aruun's home. But the recipes remember where we started.

talk.say: Ooh, I can smell 'em from here!

choices.text: Fresh redroot and reeds, as you asked.
choices.reply: Lovely and firm, every one. Here: stew while it's warm, and flatbread for the road. Don't tell Maru at the long hearth I gave you extra.

talk.say: Three fresh redroot and two vermillion reed stalks, love. Redroot grows wild in the meadows; the reeds grow along the water. I grind the seed heads for flour.
Hungry? I got somethin' good cookin'!

choices.reply: Redroot stew, the way my family's always made it. Recipe's older than this town, I'd bet.
Bless you! I'm short three fresh redroot and two vermillion reed stalks. Fresh, mind. Not the bruised ones.
Born and raised right here, love, same as my mum and her mum before her. Folk stare sometimes. Let 'em. They still come back for seconds.

talk.say: Back again? Good. Nobody leaves my stall hungry.
